messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Javier Morales, a 58-year-old forensic analyst, had always prided himself on his meticulous attention to detail and his calm, rational demeanour, qualities essential to his demanding work. That stability shattered five years ago when he was consulting at a multi-agency building downtown. Without warning, a section of the structure gave way, a catastrophic collapse that trapped dozens and filled the air with dust, screams, and the acrid smell of pulverized concrete. Javier, though physically unharmed, witnessed the immediate horror, the frantic scramble, and the agonizing wait for rescue. The sheer unexpectedness of the disaster fundamentally altered his perception, leaving him with the profound conviction that the world is a dangerous place, a belief that had only solidified with time.

In the aftermath, Javier’s internal world shifted dramatically. He soon found his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, a persistent, low-grade hum of vigilance that never truly receded. This underlying state meant he was frequently feeling jumpy or easily startled by everyday occurrences – a door slamming in the office, a sudden car horn on his commute, even his wife, Elena, moving unexpectedly in the kitchen. These reactions, alien to his former self, led him to the painful conclusion that his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, a stark contrast to the capable professional he had always been.

His discomfort extended beyond his immediate environment. What troubled him most was how this pervasive sense of threat began to dictate his movements. As a forensic analyst, his job often required site visits to various locations, some familiar, some entirely new. Now, he found himself actively avoiding going to unfamiliar places because he could no longer assess the danger. The thought of entering a new building, navigating an unknown neighbourhood, or attending a conference in an unfamiliar city filled him with an almost paralyzing apprehension. He would invent excuses, delegate tasks he once relished, and increasingly confine his work to the controlled environment of his laboratory. This retreat from professional duties he once excelled at fueled a growing internal narrative that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, eroding his self-esteem and professional identity.

This constellation of symptoms became a constant companion. At home, Elena noticed his increased irritability and his inability to relax, even during their favourite evening routines. At work, his colleagues saw him decline travel opportunities and become more withdrawn, though no one quite understood the depth of his internal struggle. Javier knew intellectually that he needed help, yet the prospect of navigating an unfamiliar therapist's office or even discussing his vulnerabilities felt like another insurmountable challenge in a world that now seemed full of hidden perils. The weight of his constant vigilance, his self-reproach, and the shrinking confines of his life finally became too much to bear, prompting him to seek the very support he had so long resisted. He arrived for his first appointment, his body on alert, hoping for some relief from the relentless fear that had become his shadow.
